title: I built a 3-step AI email drafting workflow - did it really free up time and boost my freelance earnings?

body:
## Can AI really cut the endless back-and-forth of email writing?

I was skeptical. My inbox was a constant ping-pong of drafts, revisions, and polite filler. I thought an AI could give me a decent first pass, but I also feared it would sound robotic and require more tweaking than it saved. So I built a tiny workflow, kept it to three steps, and measured both time saved and any extra cash it might bring.

### The three steps I settled on

- **Prompt library** - A plain-text file with reusable prompts for common email types: project kickoff, scope change, invoice reminder, thank-you note. Example prompt: "Write a friendly 150-word email to a client confirming the start date for a web redesign project."
- **One-click generation** - A lightweight Node.js script that calls the OpenAI API. I bound each prompt to a keyboard shortcut via Raycast. Hitting the shortcut opens the AI, feeds the prompt, and drops the raw draft into my clipboard.
- **Quick edit checklist** - A short markdown checklist in my notes reminds me to personalize the greeting, verify dates, and add any attachments. It takes less than a minute to scan before hitting send.

### How I measured the impact

I tracked two things for four weeks:

- **Time spent on email drafts** - I started a Toggl timer each time I opened a new email draft.
- **Extra earnings** - I logged any new gigs or higher rates I could directly attribute to faster communication (for example, a client accepted a proposal because I replied within an hour).

#### Time saved

Before the workflow I averaged about 12 minutes per email, including drafting, polishing, and double-checking details. After the system went live the average dropped to roughly 7 minutes. With around 15 client emails a week, that adds up to about an hour of work saved each week.

#### Money added

The time saved didn’t magically turn into cash, but the speed helped me close two small projects that might have slipped away when I was slower to reply. Those gigs added a few hundred dollars to my monthly freelance income. In my view, the real value is the mental bandwidth freed up for higher-value work.

### What actually worked (and what didn’t)

**What worked**

- Consistent prompt format - Short, focused prompts kept the AI on target.
- Keyboard shortcuts - The one-click feel removed friction; I never had to open a browser or type a long command.
- Checklist for personalization - A quick glance prevented the "generic AI" feel and kept client relationships warm.

**What fell short**

- Complex negotiations - The AI struggled with nuanced pricing language; I still wrote those from scratch.
- Tone fine-tuning - For high-stakes clients I often added a sentence or two to match their preferred style.

### Quick setup checklist (copy-paste)

- Create a prompt file - List 5-7 common email types you send.
- Hook it to a shortcut - Use Raycast, Alfred, or a simple shell script.
- Add a 3-point edit list - Greeting, date/number check, attachment reminder.
- Track time - Start a timer the first time you use the system.
- Review earnings - Note any new work that correlates with faster replies.

### A concrete example

A client asked for a quick turnaround on a logo redesign and needed confirmation of the start date. I fired the shortcut, got a draft in seconds, tweaked the greeting, and sent it within 5 minutes. The client appreciated the speed and awarded the project on the spot.

### FAQ

**Q: Do I need a paid AI plan to see these results?**
A: Not necessarily. The free tier of most large-language models gives you enough tokens for a few dozen drafts a month. Once you hit the limit, a low-cost plan unlocks unlimited use.

**Q: Will this work for non-English emails?**
A: The model handles many languages, but you’ll need to tailor prompts to the language you’re writing in. Expect a slightly higher edit rate.

**Q: Is this safe for confidential client info?**
A: Treat the AI as a drafting assistant, not a vault. Never feed sensitive contract details; keep the prompts generic and add specifics after the draft.

## Bottom line

A three-step AI email drafting workflow can shave roughly an hour off a freelancer’s week and, if you’re quick enough, translate that speed into a few hundred dollars of extra income. It’s not a silver bullet, but it’s a practical tool that removes a lot of the grunt work. Give it a try, tweak the prompts to your voice, and decide whether the time saved is worth any subscription you might need.
